Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

vignette: Malika, a 48-year-old waitress living in a bustling city, had once thrived on the energy of her job, relishing the interactions with customers and the camaraderie with her colleagues. However, a harrowing experience had stolen her joy and replaced it with a shadow that loomed over her daily life. A year ago, a former acquaintance had begun stalking her, appearing unexpectedly at her workplace and following her home. This constant violation of her personal space shattered her sense of safety. The memories of these encounters forced their way into her mind at the most inopportune times, leaving her feeling trapped in an experience that felt alien, as if it had happened to someone else entirely. After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me, reinforcing her negative appraisals about her worth and safety. The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost. Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure. In the aftermath of the stalking, Malika found herself retreating from the vibrant social life she had once cherished. This retreat was fueled by her negative belief that expressing her emotions would only lead to further pain, which made her avoid reaching out for help or sharing her struggles with others. She avoided her friends and colleagues, convinced that they could not understand the fear that had taken root within her. What frightened her most was the thought of being judged or dismissed if she revealed the depth of her misery. Her belief that expressing her emotions would only lead to further pain kept her trapped in silence, so she buried her feelings deeper, only to find they resurfaced with even greater intensity. With each passing day, she felt her happiness slip further away, leading her to believe that life held no meaning anymore. This pervasive sense of hopelessness drove her to avoid social contacts, as she could not bear to face the pity or confusion of those who used to know her as the lively person she once was. Malika's experiences had instilled a deep-seated threat perception that permeated every aspect of her life. The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair, leading her to conclude that she was no longer the person she once knew and that safety was an illusion. Having concluded that she was perpetually vulnerable, she approached every new environment with trepidation, convinced that danger lurked just beyond her sight. Having concluded that she was perpetually vulnerable, she approached every new environment with trepidation, convinced that danger lurked just beyond her sight. She avoided unfamiliar places, convinced that danger lurked around every corner. Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe. When the threat felt this close, staying home became her only rational choice; it was the only way to feel safe in a world that seemed perpetually dangerous. Her heart raced at the slightest sound, her body bracing for an intrusion that never came. Unfamiliar environments triggered a cascade of panic, forcing her to remain confined to her home, where she felt a semblance of control. Yet, even within the safety of her four walls, she could not escape the memories that haunted her, invading her thoughts when she least expected them. She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh and vivid in her mind. The memories felt like an unwanted guest; they crept in uninvited, and to keep them at bay, she buried herself in distractions, convincing herself that if she ignored them long enough, they would fade away. Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away. She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy. To cope with the vividness of these memories, she found herself constantly seeking distractions, believing that staying busy would provide a shield against the painful recollections that threatened to overwhelm her. Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it. These recollections were so vivid that she often struggled to articulate them, feeling as if they belonged to another person entirely. As time passed, Malika's emotional landscape grew increasingly desolate. The joy she once derived from her work was replaced with a profound sense of numbness, as if she were merely going through the motions. The fear of conflict had taken hold, preventing her from engaging in any situation that might lead to disagreement or confrontation. In her effort to avoid any emotional discomfort, she had developed a habit of suppressing her feelings, which paradoxically kept the memories fresh and vivid in her mind, as they remained unprocessed and unresolved. Her negative belief that expressing her emotions would only lead to further pain kept her trapped in silence, so she buried her feelings deeper, only to find they resurfaced with even greater intensity. Each day became a careful balancing act of avoidance, as she tried to quell the physical reactivity that surged within her whenever reminders of the stalking surfaced. When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible. The memories of her experience, intertwined with her growing maladaptive strategies, created an echo chamber of dread, reinforcing her belief that she was no longer the person she used to be. Her conviction that she was a burden if she shared her struggles only deepened her avoidance, leading her to isolate further, convinced that retreat was the only way to protect both herself and those around her. The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong. Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was. The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair. Malika's internal struggle became a cycle; each negative appraisal of her situation fueled her maladaptive behaviors, perpetuating the very memories she sought to escape. Her belief that she was a burden to others if she shared her feelings led her to withdraw further, reinforcing her isolation and prompting her to avoid situations that might lead to connection or understanding. She felt as though her past was a chain that weighed her down, constricting her ability to move forward. The emotional numbness she experienced left her feeling dead inside, amplifying her retreat from the world. Each time she found herself listening intently for sounds that might indicate danger, she was reminded of the life she had lost—an existence filled with laughter and connection, now overshadowed by fear and isolation. The turning point came when Malika realized that she could no longer endure this relentless cycle alone. A fleeting moment of connection with a co-worker—a simple, caring inquiry about her well-being—shook her from her stupor. It made her reflect on the lost happiness and meaning in her life and ignited a flicker of hope. She recognized that seeking help might be the key to reclaiming her sense of self and breaking free from the torment of her memories. As she sat in the therapist's office, she grappled with the fear of opening up, worried that her vulnerabilities might be dismissed or misunderstood. Still, she held onto the hope that through this journey, she could find her way back to the person she once was, or perhaps, emerge as someone even stronger.

vignette_attempts.vignette: Malika, a 48-year-old waitress living in a bustling city, had once thrived on the energy of her job, relishing the interactions with customers and the camaraderie with her colleagues. However, a harrowing experience had stolen her joy and replaced it with a shadow that loomed over her daily life. A year ago, a former acquaintance had begun stalking her, appearing unexpectedly at her workplace and following her home. This constant violation of her personal space shattered her sense of safety. The memories of these encounters forced their way into her mind at the most inopportune times, leaving her feeling trapped in an experience that felt alien, as if it had happened to someone else entirely. The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost. Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure. In the aftermath of the stalking, Malika found herself retreating from the vibrant social life she had once cherished. She avoided her friends and colleagues, convinced that they could not understand the fear that had taken root within her. What frightened her most was the thought of being judged or dismissed if she revealed the depth of her misery. Her belief that expressing her emotions would only lead to further pain kept her trapped in silence, so she buried her feelings deeper, only to find they resurfaced with even greater intensity. With each passing day, she felt her happiness slip further away, leading her to believe that life held no meaning anymore. This pervasive sense of hopelessness drove her to avoid social contacts, as she could not bear to face the pity or confusion of those who used to know her as the lively person she once was. Malika's experiences had instilled a deep-seated threat perception that permeated every aspect of her life. Having concluded that she was perpetually vulnerable, she approached every new environment with trepidation, convinced that danger lurked just beyond her sight. Having concluded that she was perpetually vulnerable, she approached every new environment with trepidation, convinced that danger lurked just beyond her sight. She avoided unfamiliar places, convinced that danger lurked around every corner. Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe. When the threat felt this close, staying home became her only rational choice; it was the only way to feel safe in a world that seemed perpetually dangerous. Her heart raced at the slightest sound, her body bracing for an intrusion that never came. Unfamiliar environments triggered a cascade of panic, forcing her to remain confined to her home, where she felt a semblance of control. Yet, even within the safety of her four walls, she could not escape the memories that haunted her, invading her thoughts when she least expected them. The memories felt like an unwanted guest; they crept in uninvited, and to keep them at bay, she buried herself in distractions, convincing herself that if she ignored them long enough, they would fade away. Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away. She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy. To cope with the vividness of these memories, she found herself constantly seeking distractions, believing that staying busy would provide a shield against the painful recollections that threatened to overwhelm her. Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it. These recollections were so vivid that she often struggled to articulate them, feeling as if they belonged to another person entirely. As time passed, Malika's emotional landscape grew increasingly desolate. The joy she once derived from her work was replaced with a profound sense of numbness, as if she were merely going through the motions. The fear of conflict had taken hold, preventing her from engaging in any situation that might lead to disagreement or confrontation. In her effort to avoid any emotional discomfort, she had developed a habit of suppressing her feelings, which paradoxically kept the memories fresh and vivid in her mind, as they remained unprocessed and unresolved. Her negative belief that expressing her emotions would only lead to further pain kept her trapped in silence, so she buried her feelings deeper, only to find they resurfaced with even greater intensity. Each day became a careful balancing act of avoidance, as she tried to quell the physical reactivity that surged within her whenever reminders of the stalking surfaced. When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible. The memories of her experience, intertwined with her growing maladaptive strategies, created an echo chamber of dread, reinforcing her belief that she was no longer the person she used to be. Her conviction that she was a burden if she shared her struggles only deepened her avoidance, leading her to isolate further, convinced that retreat was the only way to protect both herself and those around her. The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong. Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was. The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair. Malika's internal struggle became a cycle; each negative appraisal of her situation fueled her maladaptive behaviors, perpetuating the very memories she sought to escape. Her belief that she was a burden to others if she shared her feelings led her to withdraw further, reinforcing her isolation and prompting her to avoid situations that might lead to connection or understanding. She felt as though her past was a chain that weighed her down, constricting her ability to move forward. The emotional numbness she experienced left her feeling dead inside, amplifying her retreat from the world. Each time she found herself listening intently for sounds that might indicate danger, she was reminded of the life she had lost—an existence filled with laughter and connection, now overshadowed by fear and isolation. The turning point came when Malika realized that she could no longer endure this relentless cycle alone. A fleeting moment of connection with a co-worker—a simple, caring inquiry about her well-being—shook her from her stupor. It made her reflect on the lost happiness and meaning in her life and ignited a flicker of hope. She recognized that seeking help might be the key to reclaiming her sense of self and breaking free from the torment of her memories. As she sat in the therapist's office, she grappled with the fear of opening up, worried that her vulnerabilities might be dismissed or misunderstood. Still, she held onto the hope that through this journey, she could find her way back to the person she once was, or perhaps, emerge as someone even stronger.
